# Megacolon

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Megacolon*

[Original Article Link](/library/fo0kYS)

---

## Summary

Megacolon is the dilation of the <u>colon</u> in the absence of a mechanical obstruction (e.g., <u>colonic</u> <u>tumor</u>/stricture). There are three etiological types of megacolon: acute, chronic, and <u>toxic megacolon</u>. <u>Acute megacolon</u> (<u>Ogilvie's syndrome</u>) is the acute dilation of the <u>colon</u>, characteristically seen in severely medically/surgically ill patients, probably secondary to an <u>electrolyte</u>/metabolic imbalance. <u>Chronic megacolon</u> is the permanent dilation of the <u>colon</u> caused by chronic <u>colonic</u> dysmotility due to an underlying neuropathic (<u>Hirschsprung's disease</u>, chronic <u>Chagas disease</u>) or myopathic (<u>Duchenne's muscular dystrophy</u>) disorder. Patients with acute/<u>chronic megacolon</u> typically present with abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>bloating</u>, and <u>constipation</u>. <u>Toxic megacolon</u> is a life-threatening dilation of the <u>colon</u> associated with systemic toxicity due to <u>infectious colitis</u> (<u>C. difficile</u> <u>pseudomembranous colitis</u>, <u>Salmonella enterocolitis</u>) or inflammatory <u>colitis</u> (<u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>). Patients typically present with <u>signs of sepsis</u> (<u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>) and a history of abdominal <u>pain</u> and bloody <u>diarrhea</u>. Abdominal <u>x-rays</u> demonstrate a <u>colonic</u> dilation, with/without air-fluid levels, and preserved haustrae. <u>Contrast-enhanced CT scans</u> can identify/rule out a mechanical <u>colonic</u> obstruction and possible complications (<u>colonic ischemia</u>/perforation). Patients with acute/<u>chronic megacolon</u> can often be <u>treated conservatively</u> with bowel rest, dietary modifications, <u>prokinetic</u> drugs, and/or <u>neostigmine</u>. Colonoscopic decompression is often successful in patients with <u>acute megacolon</u>. Surgical intervention for acute/<u>chronic megacolon</u> (<u>colectomy</u> and ileorectal <u>anastomosis</u>) is indicated if <u>conservative treatment</u> fails. <u>Conservative management</u> of <u>toxic megacolon</u> includes bowel rest, IV <u>antibiotics</u> (for <u>infectious colitis</u>), IV <u>steroids</u> (for <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>). There is a high risk of <u>colonic</u> perforation in patients with <u>toxic megacolon</u>. Hence, no improvement to medical therapy within 24–72 hours is an indication to perform <u>surgery</u> (subtotal <u>colectomy</u> and end <u>ileostomy</u>).

---

## Acute megacolon (Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction or Ogilvie's syndrome)

* Description: acute dilation of the <u>colon</u> in the absence of a mechanical obstruction, characteristically seen in severely ill or postoperative patients [[2]](/library/wm0h3g)[[3]](/library/9m0N3g)

* Etiology

* Occurs in seriously ill patients or those who have undergone a major surgical procedure

* <u>Idiopathic</u>; possible factors include:

* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalance

* Major <u>surgery</u> (e.g., orthopedic, <u>pelvic</u>, or cardiothoracic <u>surgery</u>)

* Trauma (e.g, <u>fractures</u> of <u>long bones</u>, <u>spinal cord injury</u>)

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u>

* Drugs which are known to decrease intestinal motility (e.g., <u>anticholinergic drugs</u>, <u>opioid analgesics</u>, <u>antipsychotics</u>, <u>calcium channel blockers</u>)

* Pathophysiology: etiological factors → impairment/destruction of the autonomic nervous system → imbalance between <u>sympathetic</u> and <u>parasympathetic</u> control of intestinal motility → accumulation of feces, air, and intestinal secretions in the intestine → <u>colonic</u> dilation

* Clinical features

* Gradual abdominal distention

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>; <u>constipation</u>/<u>diarrhea</u>

* Tympanitic <u>abdominal percussion</u>; decreased frequency of <u>bowel sounds</u>

* Signs of <u>colonic ischemia</u> or impending perforation: <u>Fever</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, and <u>peritoneal signs</u> (guarding, rigidity, <u>rebound tenderness</u>)

* Diagnostics

* <u>Laboratory values</u>

* May show signs of underlying disease

* <u>Hypokalemia</u> as a potential cause

* <u>Abdominal x-ray</u> 

* Dilation of the <u>cecum</u> and right <u>colon</u> (occasionally up to the <u>rectum</u>) with/without multiple <u>air-fluid levels</u>

* Haustrae are preserved

* <u>Contrast enhanced CT scan</u> (oral and IV contrast)  [[4]](/library/xm0E3g)

* Confirms <u>x-ray</u> findings

* Rules out mechanical obstruction (e.g., <u>tumor</u>/stricture)

* Can diagnose complications (<u>ischemic</u> bowel segments or perforation <u>peritonitis</u>)

* <u>Colonoscopy</u> and endoscopy

* Indicated in hemodynamically stable patients when <u>CECT</u> cannot be performed

* Rules out a mechanical obstruction

* Colonoscopic decompression can be performed in the same sitting.

* Treatment  [[5]](/library/Cm0q3g)

* Supportive measures

* Bowel decompression

* <u>Nasogastric tube</u> to decompress the <u>stomach</u>

* <u>Rectal tube</u> to decompress the <u>rectum</u> and <u>distal</u> <u>colon</u>

* <u>IV fluids</u> and bowel rest (<u>NPO</u>)

* Treat the inciting factor (e.g., stop the offending drug, correct the <u>electrolyte</u> abnormality.

* Indicated in patients with mild symptoms and cecal dilation < 12 cm

* Pharmacologic management: <u>Neostigmine</u> 

* Indicated when no improvement > 24–48 hours of bowel rest and decompression and/or cecal dilation > 12 cm with no signs of <u>colonic ischemia</u>/perforation or <u>peritonitis</u>

* Treatment with <u>methylnaltrexone</u> may be attempted if <u>opiates</u> are suspected as a precipitating factor.

* Intervention/<u>surgery</u>

* Indications

* Signs of impending or actual <u>colonic ischemia</u>/perforation or <u>peritonitis</u>

* Failure of <u>conservative therapy</u>

* Colonoscopic bowel decompression: indicated if <u>neostigmine</u> is contraindicated or unsuccessful  [[6]](/library/Dm013g)

* <u>Cecostomy</u>

* <u>Colectomy</u> with/without <u>colostomy</u>

## Chronic megacolon (chronic colonic pseudo-obstruction)

* Description: Permanent dilation of the <u>colon</u> caused by congenital/acquired <u>colonic</u> dysmotility in the absence of a mechanical obstruction [[7]](/library/-m0DRg)

* Etiology

* Congenital (e.g., <u>Hirschsprung disease</u>)

* Acquired

* Neuropathies (e.g., <u>diabetic neuropathy</u>, <u>spinal cord injury</u>, <u>Parkinson's disease</u>) [[8]](/library/Y50nig)

* <u>Myopathies</u> (e.g., <u>Duchenne's muscular dystrophy</u>, <u>myotonic muscular dystrophy</u>)

* <u>Connective tissue disorders</u> (e.g., <u>scleroderma</u>, <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>, <u>dermatomyositis</u>)

* Chronic <u>Chagas disease</u>   [[9]](/library/Z50Zig)

* <u>Idiopathic</u> - reason unknown  [[10]](/library/050eig)

* Pathophysiology: Etiological factors cause a neural and/or motor dysfunction of the bowel → bowel dysmotility  → progressive <u>colonic</u> dilation  [[7]](/library/-m0DRg)

* Clinical features

* Recurrent episodes of: 

* <u>Constipation</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> and distention (<u>bloating</u>)

* <u>Anorexia</u>, early satiety, and <u>nausea</u>

* Examination findings: Abdominal distention; mild abdominal tenderness

* Signs and symptoms of the underlying disorder

* Diagnostics

* <u>Laboratory values</u>: may show signs of underlying disease

* <u>Abdominal x-ray</u> may show: 

* Dilation of the <u>cecum</u> and right <u>colon</u> (occasionally up to the <u>rectum</u>) with/without multiple <u>air-fluid levels</u>

* Haustrae are preserved

* <u>Contrast-enhanced CT scan</u> (<u>CECT</u>; oral and IV contrast)

* Confirms <u>x-ray</u> findings

* Rules out mechanical obstruction (e.g., <u>tumor</u>/stricture)

* Can diagnose complications (<u>ischemic</u> bowel segments or perforation <u>peritonitis</u>)  [[4]](/library/xm0E3g)

* <u>Colonoscopy</u> and endoscopy: indicated in hemodynamically stable patients when <u>CECT</u> cannot be performed; rules out a mechanical obstruction

* <u>Colon transit studies</u>: to assess <u>colonic</u> motility  [[11]](/library/Bm0z3g)[[12]](/library/ym0dRg)[[13]](/library/Am0RRg)

* <u>Colon transit scintigraphy</u>: Investigation of choice to diagnose and determine the extent of delayed <u>colonic</u> transit  [[12]](/library/ym0dRg)[[13]](/library/Am0RRg)

* <u>Colon</u> transit test using <u>radio-opaque</u> markers  [[11]](/library/Bm0z3g)

* <u>Wireless motility capsule test</u>  [[11]](/library/Bm0z3g)[[14]](/library/2GYTAq)

* Manometry

* <u>Colonic</u> <u>biopsy</u>

* Treatment [[1]](/library/8m0Ohg)[[15]](/library/a50Qig)

* <u>Conservative management</u> 

* Dietary modifications

* <u>Osmotic laxatives</u> and enemas to empty the <u>colon</u> and prevent <u>fecal impaction</u>

* <u>Prokinetic</u> drugs: <u>Erythromycin</u>, <u>metoclopramide</u>, <u>neostigmine</u>

* Treatment of the underlying disorder

* <u>Surgery</u>: indicated in patients who do not improve/worsen on <u>conservative therapy</u>

* <u>Total abdominal colectomy</u> with ileorectal <u>anastomosis</u>

* See "Surgical treatment" of <u>Hirschsprung's disease</u>

## Toxic megacolon

* Description: a life-threatening, acute dilation of the <u>colon</u> associated with systemic toxicity

* Etiology

* <u>Infectious colitis</u>

* Bacterial: <u>C. difficile</u> (<u>pseudomembranous colitis</u>), <u>Salmonella</u>, <u>Shigella</u>, <u>Campylobacter</u> infections

* Parasitic: <u>Trypanosoma cruzi</u> (<u>Chagas disease</u>), <u>E. histolytica</u> (<u>amebic dysentery</u>) infections

* Inflammatory <u>colitis</u>: <u>Ulcerative colitis</u>, <u>Crohn disease</u>

* Pathophysiology: <u>colitis</u> (inflammation)

* <u>Colonic</u> accumulation of inflammatory mediators and bacteria → <u>nitric oxide</u> synthesis → <u>colonic</u> dilation [[16]](/library/c50aQg)

* <u>Edema</u> and inflammation of the <u>colonic</u> <u>smooth muscle</u> → <u>colonic</u> dysmotility → <u>colonic</u> dilation

* Clinical features

* (Bloody) <u>diarrhea</u> and <u>vomiting</u>

* Abdominal distention and <u>pain</u>

* Signs of <u>sepsis</u> (<u>fever</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>) and <u>dehydration</u>

* Signs of underlying disease (See <u>Ulcerative colitis</u>, <u>Crohn disease</u>)

* Diagnostics

* Laboratory findings

* <u>Neutrophilic leukocytosis</u>

* <u>Anemia</u>

* ↑ <u>ESR</u>/<u>CRP</u>

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* Abdominal <u>x-ray</u> findings  

* Dilation of the <u>colon</u> (<u>transverse colon</u> diameter > 6 cm)

* Loss of haustration

* Multiple <u>air-fluid levels</u>

* Contrast enhanced <u>CT scan</u> (oral and IV contrast)

* Confirms <u>x-ray</u> findings

* Rules out mechanical obstruction (e.g., <u>tumor</u>/stricture)

* Can diagnose complications (<u>ischemic</u> bowel segments or perforation <u>peritonitis</u>)  [[4]](/library/xm0E3g)

* Stool tests for <u>C. difficile</u> toxin: in patients with preceding <u>diarrhea</u> (see "Diagnosis" of <u>clostridium difficile infection</u>)

* <u>Colonoscopy</u> and endoscopy: contraindicated in suspected <u>toxic megacolon</u> due to high risk of perforating the <u>colon</u>

* Diagnostic criteria

* Radiographic evidence of <u>colonic</u> dilatation

* Three of the following: <u>fever</u> (> 38.6Â°C (> 101.5Â°F)), <u>tachycardia</u> (> 120 beats/min), <u>leukocytosis</u> (> 10,500/Î¼L), or <u>anemia</u>

* One of the following: <u>dehydration</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, <u>altered mental status</u>, or <u>electrolyte</u> disturbance

* Treatment

* <u>Conservative treatment</u> [[17]](/library/vJYADJ)[[18]](/library/DJY1wJ)

* Admission to <u>intensive care unit</u>

* <u>Complete bowel rest</u>: <u>NPO</u>

* <u>Nasogastric tube insertion</u>

* <u>IV fluids</u>

* Correction of fluid and <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances

* <u>Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>ampicillin</u>, <u>gentamicin</u>, and <u>metronidazole</u>)
* Oral <u>vancomycin</u> or <u>fidaxomicin</u> for <u>C. difficile colitis</u>

* Rotation techniques: change position frequently to facilitate the evacuation of bowel gas (<u>prone</u> or knee-<u>elbow</u> position)

* Avoid all <u>anticholinergic</u> or narcotic medications

* IV <u>steroids</u> (<u>hydrocortisone</u>, <u>dexamethasone</u>) for <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Indications: no response to medical management within 24–72 hours; development of complications

* Procedure: subtotal <u>colectomy</u> and end <u>ileostomy</u>

* Complications

* <u>Colonic ischemia</u> → <u>colonic</u> perforation→ <u>peritonitis</u>

* <u>Sepsis</u> and <u>multiorgan dysfunction</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Colonoscopy</u> should be avoided in patients with suspected <u>toxic megacolon</u> since it increases the risk of <u>colonic</u> perforation.
